references.text: Pharaoh had previously summoned Moses and Aaron back to negotiate who should be allowed to go to worship the Lord.
Pharaoh continues to negotiate and limit who may go to serve the Lord; this time, he wants to keep the livestock behind.
Moses and Aaron's original request to Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go to hold a feast for the Lord in the wilderness.
Pharaoh tries to restrict the Israelites' worship by suggesting they offer sacrifices within the land instead of going out.
Finally, Pharaoh sends all the people of Israel out, including men, women, children, and livestock—the opposite of his earlier restriction here.
Pharaoh drives Moses away from his presence and threatens him with death if he returns.
Both verses mark critical turning points in the confrontation where Pharaoh angrily drives God's people away, first as a compromise attempt and later as total capitulation.
The verses illustrate the contrast between Pharaoh's compromising offer of partial service and God's uncompromising demand for full liberation to serve Him.
A profound theological contrast: Pharaoh drives Moses away from his presence in anger, while God later must send His own people away from His presence because of their disobedience.
1 Samuel 6:6 uses the event in Exodus (including the scene where Pharaoh drove them away) as a theological example of stubbornness and God's power.
The verses connect Moses' warning against Pharaoh's deception with the actual event where Pharaoh tried to change the terms of their departure.
